title: Pinterest and Intel Take Open-Source Profiling to Internet Scale
gist: Pinterest partnered with Intel to extend the open-source continuous profiler gProfiler for its fleet of hundreds of thousands of instances serving 640 million MAUs, adding remotely triggered dynamic profiling, Intel PerfSpect hardware telemetry, PMC flame graphs and wall-time profiling, and contributing the work upstream instead of building a proprietary tool.

insights.claim: Pinterest runs hundreds of thousands of instances serving 640 million monthly active users across Java, Python, C++, Go and Node.js, where even small efficiency gains carry significant infrastructure cost implications.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Profiling-driven efficiency is a margin lever for large internet platforms' infrastructure spend.
insights.locator: Pinterest claims it operates hundreds of thousands of instances

insights.claim: Pinterest replaced fragmented use of perf, async-profiler and py-spy with gProfiler, an orchestration layer that merges system-wide perf data with runtime-specific profilers into a unified flame graph per host without code changes.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Orchestrating existing open-source profilers is the cheaper path versus proprietary platforms.
insights.locator: gProfiler acts as an orchestration layer

insights.claim: Pinterest chose to extend open-source gProfiler with Intel and contribute back rather than build a proprietary profiling platform or adapt Intel VTune, which was designed as a performance-engineering tool rather than a cloud-native fleet profiler.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Intel is using open-source software contributions to embed its hardware telemetry into hyperscale ops tooling.

insights.claim: gProfiler's new dynamic profiling lets engineers trigger profiling remotely on services, hosts or clusters via UI or API, with dormant agents consuming under 1% CPU and 100 MB of memory and taking instructions via heartbeats.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Low-overhead always-on agents make continuous profiling economically viable at fleet scale.

insights.claim: Integration with Intel PerfSpect gives gProfiler hardware-level data such as cache behaviour, memory bandwidth and CPU stalls, and new PMC flame graphs correlate functions with hardware events like cache misses and branch mispredictions.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Hardware-aware profiling ties software efficiency work to CPU vendor tooling, a soft lock-in channel for Intel.

insights.claim: Wall-time profiling was added because services can be slow while using little CPU when threads wait on I/O, locks or RPCs, which CPU profiling cannot reveal.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Latency diagnosis in microservices needs wall-time visibility beyond CPU sampling.

insights.claim: gProfiler Performance Studio stores profiles in S3, uses SQS for asynchronous indexing and ClickHouse for analytical queries, with a React frontend, and was hardened for multi-terabyte ingestion before fleet deployment.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: ClickHouse continues to win observability-analytics backends at internet scale.

insights.claim: gProfiler competes in a crowded continuous-profiling market with eBPF-based Parca and Grafana Pyroscope and commercial platforms such as Datadog, differentiating on system-wide multi-runtime orchestration and hardware-level profiling.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Open-source profilers backed by large users pressure commercial observability pricing (e.g., Datadog).
insights.locator: gProfiler sits in an increasingly crowded

insights.claim: At Pinterest's scale, waiting for engineers to reproduce problems or manually profile machines is too costly, so continuous profiling becomes a baseline layer of production observability with dynamic profiling for anomalies.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Profiling is shifting from ad hoc debugging to a standard observability pillar, expanding the market.
